patients.label: 6-year-old spayed female Goldendoodle with high-grade second-degree AV block and atrial flutter and suspected atropine-induced delirium

identity_evidence.quote: A 6-year-old spayed female Goldendoodle was presented as a referral for bradycardia and collapse.

attribution_limitations: The authors considered that lidocaine could have contributed to the altered mental state but judged cumulative atropine more likely, and note the patient may have been sensitive to the drug; the cause of the suspected delirium is not established.
The abstract gives the intended pacemaker placement as the following morning, while the case text says the following day; neither gives a clock time.
The mydriasis and reduced pupillary light response are described as suspected to be secondary to residual atropine effects; this is a suspicion, not a stated diagnosis.
The case text reports mild four-chamber dilation on the echocardiogram (suspected secondary to chronic bradycardia), while the discussion says the echocardiogram revealed no structural abnormalities.

limitations: The source lists no figures, tables or supplements, so no pixel or supplement review applies.
Institution names are redacted as XXX in the source and the hospital name is not stored.
Discussion paragraphs on atropine pharmacology, human and other-species delirium and glycopyrrolate are general and were not copied to the patient.
No calendar dates are given; times are relative to the described events only.

claims.text: A 6-year-old spayed female Goldendoodle was referred to a veterinary cardiology service for bradycardia after four episodes of collapse over a 2-week period, with no neurological signs noted at home. She was bradycardic with an irregular rhythm; the electrocardiogram showed atrial flutter with high-grade second-degree atrioventricular block, thoracic radiographs were unremarkable, and the echocardiogram showed mild four-chamber dilation. She was hospitalized overnight on telemetry with pacemaker placement planned.

claims.text: To rule out high vagal tone, atropine 0.04 mg/kg and lidocaine 2 mg/kg were given intravenously twice, one hour apart, without ECG response; causes of increased vagal tone were ruled out. An atropine CRI was started at 0.02 mg/kg/h and increased to 0.04 mg/kg/h for progressive bradycardia.
